face-touching-phone-hygiene-habit.text: Skincare communities suggest wiping phones, washing pillowcases and keeping hands off the face to cut down on breakouts and keep skin clearer. It is a low-effort routine, and its effect on acne has not been tested directly.

minimalist-routine-gentle-cleanser-moist.text: Users strip their routine to a gentle cleanser and moisturizer to avoid irritating the skin barrier, aiming for calmer, less breakout-prone skin. The approach is consistent with general dermatology guidance on the barrier, though the minimalist routine itself has not been trialled for acne.

silicone-onion-extract-scar-gel-mederma.text: Mederma and silicone gels or sheets are used to make scars look softer and less noticeable, including acne and surgical scars. Silicone products have a body of scar research behind them, while trials of the onion extract gel found results similar to petrolatum.

subcision.text: Subcision is a clinic procedure used to lift rolling acne scars by releasing the fibrous bands pulling them down, giving a smoother surface. Evidence consists mostly of small studies, and forum claims that it beats other scar treatments or can be done at home are anecdotal.

chain: Skin rebuilds collagen in the pit
tca-cross.text: TCA CROSS is used by dermatologists to improve narrow, deep icepick acne scars by applying strong acid to individual scars. Small trials report improvement, including in darker skin types, with no large controlled studies.

chain: Deep scar cut out or lifted
punch-excision-punch-elevation.text: Punch excision and elevation are used on deep boxcar acne scars, either removing the scar or raising its base to skin level. The techniques are long established in dermatology, with limited trial-level data.

phenol-baker-gordon-peel.text: The phenol or Baker-Gordon peel is the deepest classic chemical peel, used for coarse wrinkling, sun damage and some scarring to resurface the skin. It is performed under medical supervision, and its results are documented mainly in older clinical reports.

prp-microneedling-vampire-facial.text: The vampire facial pairs microneedling with a person's own platelet-rich plasma for skin rejuvenation and acne scarring. Microneedling itself is studied for scars, while the added benefit of PRP is considered unproven, and claims of quick scar clearance are anecdotal.

exosome-treatments.text: Exosome serums are applied after microneedling and marketed for rejuvenation, scars, under-eye concerns and hair. Exosome biology is well studied in labs, while cosmetic use on skin remains largely untested.

picosecond-laser-picosure-picoway.text: Picosecond lasers are used in clinics for pigment, tattoos, texture and acne scars, aiming for smoother and more even skin. Small prospective studies report scar improvement, with few large trials.

nd-yag-q-switched-laser.text: Q-switched Nd:YAG lasers are used by clinics for pigmented lesions and tattoos, and appearance communities discuss them for post-acne dark marks, melasma and redness. Evidence for these appearance uses comes mostly from small trials.

pulsed-dye-laser-for-red-scars.text: Pulsed dye laser is used by dermatologists to fade red scars by targeting the blood vessels within them, and appearance circles discuss it for red acne scars. Trials exist but are small.

dermabrasion.text: Dermabrasion is a surgical resurfacing procedure used to reduce acne scars and deep surgical scars, and was the older standard before lasers. Evidence is mostly small trials.

microdermabrasion-hydrafacial.text: Microdermabrasion and HydraFacial are light exfoliating facials used for a smoother, brighter complexion and a fresh look that is visible right after treatment. Results are temporary, and published efficacy data are sparse.

nanofat-autologous-fat-grafting.text: Nanofat and fat grafting move a person's own fat to scars or areas of volume loss to improve skin quality and fill depressions. Published work is mostly small clinical series.

intralesional-steroid-5-fu-for-keloids.text: Clinicians inject corticosteroid, sometimes with 5-fluorouracil, into raised keloid scars to flatten them and reduce itch. It is a standard dermatology procedure, with limited comparative evidence between options.

scar-massage.text: Scar massage is used on healed scars to improve texture, flexibility and appearance, and clinics commonly recommend it. Evidence of benefit is weak.

vitamin-e-oil-bio-oil.text: Vitamin E oil and Bio-Oil are popular over-the-counter products used to fade scars and stretch marks. Reviews of the evidence have not supported the scar-fading claims.

rosehip-oil.text: Rosehip oil is promoted for fading scars and stretch marks and improving skin appearance. Lab and small studies exist, but clear human scar trials were not found.

lemon-juice-baking-soda-on-scars.text: Do-it-yourself pastes of lemon juice and baking soda circulate as a way to lighten or smooth scars. The practice rests on anecdote, with no clinical studies found.

pore-strips.text: Pore strips are used on the nose to peel off blackhead plugs, leaving a visibly cleaner surface straight away. The effect is temporary, and there is little clinical research.

pore-vacuum.text: Pore vacuums are handheld suction gadgets used to pull blackheads from pores for clearer-looking skin. No clinical trials back or refute the claim.

chain: Less shine and oil in pores
clay-mask-for-pores.text: Clay masks with kaolin or bentonite are used to absorb oil and make pores look smaller and skin look matte. The oil-absorbing action is plausible, while the effect on pore size is untested.

chain: Cold splash or ice on face
cold-water-ice-to-close-pores.text: Splashing the face with cold water or rubbing ice on it is a long-circulating idea for closing pores and tightening the look of skin. The belief is based on tradition, and no trials have tested it.

micropigmentation-scar-tattooing.text: Micropigmentation, or paramedical tattooing, is raised in looksmaxxing discussions as a way to blend pale or discolored scars with the surrounding skin, with the color change visible once pigment is placed. It is established in medical use, with little formal evidence summarized.

enzyme-peel-papaya-pumpkin.text: Papaya and pumpkin enzyme peels are used as a gentler alternative to acid peels for smoother, brighter skin and softer texture. A lab study found most tested products had little enzyme activity, and skin trials are lacking.

tretinoin-microneedling-stack.text: Appearance forums combine prescription tretinoin with microneedling to improve acne scars, texture and signs of aging. Each part has supporting evidence on its own, while the combination has not been studied.

baby-botox-preventative-botox.text: Younger users get small botulinum toxin doses in the hope of stopping forehead and frown lines from etching in. Botox smooths existing movement lines, but the preventive benefit is untested.

botox-alternatives-dysport-xeomin-jeuvea.text: Dysport, Xeomin, Jeuveau, Daxxify and Letybo are botulinum toxin products used like Botox to soften frown lines and other expression wrinkles. They share the same basic mechanism, and clinical trials support their use on glabellar lines.

topical-botox-creams.text: Argireline-style peptide creams are sold as a needle-free alternative to Botox for smoothing wrinkles. Evidence for wrinkle effects is thin, and skin penetration is limited.
